# Status of approved funding proposals: adding host countries in respect of FP086 (Green Cities Facility)

## Summary

This document presents the request for the addition of host countries to FP086 (Green Cities Facility) originally approved at the twenty-first meeting of the Board for the consideration of the Board.

### III. Assessment

The request from the accredited entity that will enable it to expand the programme is part of a set of programmes changes to allow EBRD to accelerate the deployment of the programme, while due diligence on other identified projects continues. The Secretariat is supporting the expansion of the programme by facilitating the inclusion of additional countries under the programme such that the programme can achieve its target outcomes and objectives.

The accredited entity, in consultation with the NIBs of the host countries, has sought to include additional countries as part of this process. These are the same countries with which NIBs of all current host countries (see annex II and annex V). The accredited entity has received seven NIBs from the nine existing host countries, and six additional NIBs from the Secretariat recommend that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.
edited entity has received seven NIBs from the nine existing host countries, and six additional NIBs from the Secretariat recommend that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.

In line with previous instances where accredited entities requested host countries to be included in the programme, the Secretariat has prepared this document, which includes the NOIs from the NIBs from seven of the nine host countries, and the NOIs from all six additional countries. The Secretariat recommends that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.

### IV. Compliance with GCF policies

In submitting this document for Board consideration, the Secretariat confirms that all relevant requirements contained in the GCF Policy on Restructuring and Cancellation have been complied with as the changes have been assessed as non-major and NDA consultation has taken place.

ents contained in the GCF Policy on Restructuring and Cancellation have been complied with as the changes have been assessed as non-major and NDA consultation has taken place.

The COVID-19 crisis put significant pressure on city finances in these countries. Consequently, cities are facing constraints to borrow and invest in climate technologies, particularly given their initial premiums. When the pandemic first hit in 2020, many cities were already facing financial pressures due to the economic downturns in their countries. For example, in 2021, cities started to recover in 2022, but need support to ensure a green recovery as they started to face new challenges including inflation and supply chain disruptions.

In addition, some of these cities are also facing political instability with neighbouring countries being the bearing the brunt of the crisis through the destruction of infrastructure and, in conflict-free areas, the prevention of access to essential services. This has led to a significant increase in energy prices for electricity, gas, and fuel in significant oil, gas and food price increases. This mainly affects countries with close economic relations to Russia and Ukraine. ## Strategic context for improving resilience and adaptation

Regardless of strained budgets, cities increasingly recognize that resilience and climate adaptation is a priority area for investment. The threat of extreme weather events has become more acute across all regions of the world, particularly in developing countries where cities grow at unprecedented speed. Both extreme weather events and climate projections indicate that urban areas will be disproportionately affected by climate change.
in developing countries where cities grow at unprecedented speed. Both extreme weather events and climate projections indicate that urban areas will be disproportionately affected by climate change. This is especially true in Mongolia, which is extremely vulnerable to climate change-induced challenges: the devastating 2014 floods in the Western Balkans and Serbia in particular which triggered a wave of displacement and migration; the severe droughts in East Africa; the extreme heat waves in Europe; and the devastating Mongolian winter that killed livestock in large numbers, forcing rural population to migrate and lead up residence in informal urban settlements.
he extreme heat waves in Europe; and the devastating Mongolian winter that killed livestock in large numbers, forcing rural population to migrate and lead up residence in informal urban settlements.

CMIP5’s climate data, which underpins the latest IPCC Assessment report and which has been synthesised by the World Bank into country briefs, is unequivocal: the mountainous Western Balkans are likely to suffer more severe floods and landslides due to heavy precipitation events; East Africa will experience increased frequency of extreme heat waves and droughts; Europe faces a combination of increasing water stress, wildfires and higher mean temperatures – which is expected to put pressure on agricultural production in the Mediterranean and the Central Asian nations; extreme heat events are projected to have strong knock-on effects on droughts and food security.
pected to put pressure on agricultural production in the Mediterranean and the Central Asian nations; extreme heat events are projected to have strong knock-on effects on droughts and food security.

Climate related events threaten social and economic development, with urban poor, living in substandard housing or informal settlements, being particularly vulnerable. The Western Balkans and East Africa are among the regions most affected by climate change and high priority for cities. As a result, beneficiary cities have expressed strong demand for support for adaptation projects. A first GCF investment grant was signed in Georgia in January 2013 for the modernisation of Tbilisi metro and two additional grants have been signed in Serbia (Belgrade) and Kosovo (Pristina). The project in Ulaanbaatar Green Affordable Housing A is also being developed utilising almost all non-renewable funds available under Component 2.

# Status of approved funding proposals: adding host countries in respect of FP086 (Green Cities Facility)

## Summary

This document presents the request for the addition of host countries to FP086 (Green Cities Facility) originally approved at the twenty-first meeting of the Board for the consideration of the Board.

### III. Assessment

The request from the accredited entity that will enable it to expand the programme is part of a set of programmes changes to allow EBRD to accelerate the deployment of the programme, while due diligence on other identified projects continues. The Secretariat is supporting the expansion of the programme by facilitating the inclusion of additional countries under the programme such that the programme can achieve its target outcomes and objectives.

The accredited entity, in consultation with the NIBs of the host countries, has sought to include additional countries as part of this process. These are the same countries with which NIBs of all current host countries (see annex II and annex V). The accredited entity has received seven NIBs from the nine existing host countries, and six additional NIBs from the Secretariat recommend that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.
edited entity has received seven NIBs from the nine existing host countries, and six additional NIBs from the Secretariat recommend that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.

In line with previous instances where accredited entities requested host countries to be included in the programme, the Secretariat has prepared this document, which includes the NOIs from the NIBs from seven of the nine host countries, and the NOIs from all six additional countries. The Secretariat recommends that the Board take note of the inclusion and approve the request.

### IV. Compliance with GCF policies

In submitting this document for Board consideration, the Secretariat confirms that all relevant requirements contained in the GCF Policy on Restructuring and Cancellation have been complied with as the changes have been assessed as non-major and NDA consultation has taken place.

The EBCG seeks to expand the geographical scope of countries eligible under the Funded Activity: IP086 "Green Cities Facility" (the "Facility").

The difficult global context has profoundly affected cities. Still, in the recovery phase of the lasting impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, cities have been further impacted by the war on Ukraine and the resulting energy crisis, as well as displaced refugee communities. The EBCG is committed to supporting cities in this challenging environment. In a context of the unavoidable impact of externalities, new priorities emerge and strained budgets, it is more critical than ever.

In this context of increased needs, high uncertainty and new challenges for cities, the expansion of the geographical scope of the Facility will allow EBRD to:
dgets, it is more critical than ever.

In this context of increased needs, high uncertainty and new challenges for cities, the expansion of the geographical scope of the Facility will allow EBRD to:

- (i) support a larger group of cities; and
- (ii) accelerate the deployment of the Facility by providing timely financial support to the projects which have reached maturity, while providing critical technical assistance for those under preparation.

The EBCG seeks to increase the geographical scope of the Facility to six new countries and their cities:

* Bosnia and Herzegovina - Sarajevo
* Georgia - Tbilisi, Kutaisi, Rustavi, Gori, Mtskheta-Mtianeti, Zugdidi
* Kazakhstan - Almaty, Shymkent, Ust-Kamenogorsk
* Kyrgyz Republic - Bishkek

## Barriers for Service Providers

### Climate-smart rice farming is at its nascent stage in Thailand: aspects of the emission and/or mitigation potential of climate-smart farming have been posted or synthesised, rolled-out by foundation projects, but baseline projects, but they have not been promoted and disseminated at a large scale nor in an integrated manner. The lack of awareness among farmers about the benefits of climate-smart technology and equipment carries substantial risk due to the unclear business case (particularly for smallholder farmers) compared with the well-established and well-understood sugar cane service provider sector. There is also a perception that the climate-smart rice service provision model is not financially viable, compared with the well-established and well-understood sugar cane service provider sector.

### Financial Barriers

105. Access to finance for smallholder farmers and SME service providers can be challenging, as banks tend to be cautious and reluctant to lend to marginal clients who are already exposed to volatile weather conditions and/or have limited access to land or other collateral (e.g., livestock) for rice. Many rice farmers, and notably women farmers, earning barely a subsistence income struggle to meet their basic needs and cannot afford to pay interest rates on loans. Small-scale farmers (who own less than 10 ha of land), may not produce sufficient annual income, or may be insolvent as a result of other debts used to leverage agricultural inputs. In addition, smallholder farmers are often reluctant to borrow from service providers as farmers themselves and hence face the same challenges.

106. Existing agricultural loan products are not suitable for climate-smart agriculture. The transition from business-as-usual agriculture to climate-smart agriculture takes place over a number of years. LLL, for example, requires 5–7 years before it can be harvested. As such, farmers will need to make repeat applications in the following 4 years; the annual yield increase enabled by LLL is not sufficient to offset interest payments on loans taken out at the beginning of the project period (i.e., the baseline). These cashflow profiles call for medium-term loans with an initial grace period when climate-smart practices are still being established and yields are low.

## Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel

### 1. Overview

#### 1.1 Overview

This is a five-year project on rice farming in Thailand, targeting 21 provinces in the three most important rice-growing regions of the country: the north, the northeast and the east (see map). The project will be implemented by the Department of Agriculture for rice farming in Thailand. As such, it is a cross-cutting, medium-term project with a dual objective:

(a) To adapt rice farming in Thailand to order to reduce the negative impacts of observed and anticipated climate change conditions; and

(b) To reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions resulting from rice farming in order to help mitigate climate change.
ce the negative impacts of observed and anticipated climate change conditions; and

(b) To reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions resulting from rice farming in order to help mitigate climate change.

To achieve these objectives, the intention of this project is to intervene on three main components:

(a) Increasing the income and food security of climate-smart farmers operating under changing climatic conditions (Outcome 1);

(b) Substantially reducing GHG emissions (Outcome 2); and

(c) Directing or channeling government policies and appropriate funds towards climate-smart rice farming (Outcome 3).

With these three components, for farmers, and for soil, water and air quality, the project's three fundamental axes will be realized through:

(a) Rice farmers' adoption of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies and practices (Outcome 1);

(b) Service providers' supply of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies (Outcome 2); and
Rice farmers' adoption of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies and practices (Outcome 1);

(b) Service providers' supply of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies (Outcome 2); and

(c) Strengthening of the institutional and business environment for climate-smart rice farming.

From this perspective, the project's outcomes and outputs focus on the fundamental components that will enable the transformation towards a more sustainable and resilient productivity of Thailand’s rice farming (through climate-smart practices and technologies) and its adaptive capacity (through institutional strengthening, improved market conditions and mastery of climate change knowledge). The adoption of these technologies and practices will also enable a low-GHG emission system.

## The Thai Rice Project Will

The Thai Rice Project will enable climate-smart rice farmers—increasingly, women farmers—to adapt to a changing climate (Outcome 1) while simultaneously reducing GHG emissions (Outcome 2).

### Project Design and Outcomes

However, if the project has a high energy savings potential, the addition of some retrofit of some energy uses in buildings might yield returns in 3 to 5 years and be very attractive to investors. The key is to have a strong policy framework that ensures these projects are financially viable.

Overall ARCAFIM Approach: Rural small producers are responsible for estimated average of 80% of food production in Sub-Saharan African countries**, while MSMEs involved in food systems provide services and value-added products to the rural population. Due to their limited access to resources, financial capital, economic, social and political factors, these small producers and MSMEs disproportionately experience the effects of climate change. Despite their significant contribution to global food production and agricultural productivity, they urgently need dedicated investment resources to build stronger resilience to climate change, but have been unable to access them due to a lack of collateral and other financial constraints.

The Financial Mechanism (ARCAFIM) will address these barriers causing limited CC financing from formal financial sector lenders. ARCAFIM seeks to provide a viable alternative by providing access to finance for small producers via the mainstream private financial sector in each participating country combined with targeted technical support delivered through the project. ## B.5. Justification for GCF funding request (max 1000 words, approximately 2 pages)

The aggregate financing shortfall needed to achieve global water security has been estimated at US$37 billion by 2030 and $48 billion by 2050. These figures are based on the assumption that most investments in water infrastructure are typically financed by the public sector, but there is consensus that public finances alone are insufficient to cater to the vast investments needed for water security.

The intensity and frequency of droughts, extreme rainfall events and wildfires across South Africa have increased significantly in recent years. This has led to a shift from the current water management model that treats these trends as an anomaly towards a new water management model which identifies these trends as ongoing and persistent. This will likely affect livelihoods, food and water security as well as ecosystem services.

# Implementation arrangement

## Oversight Unit

Pegasus, as Approved Entity for the GCF, will take on the oversight role for the Equity funds received. Pegasus will either administer the GCF Equity funds and provide for the appropriate implementing arrangements with R20 and Gold Standard as EEs. Pegasus will review progress as reported by the EE to determine how best to maximize project performance. Pegasus will review projects against work plans, financial statements, and other relevant information provided by the EE. Pegasus will also have adequate skills that further analyzes technical and financial issues. Pegasus will also serve as a support and resource for the EEs in their implementation of the Equity funds and ensure its direction enhances likelihood of achieving outcomes and impact, and efficiency.

Detailed information can be found in Annex 26 (Organization) and Annex 29 (Structure).

### Organization (Annex 26)

- Pegasus will provide fund investment processes, fund management expert services and portfolio management and administrative services. lementation will be laid out in the FAA.

Éléments probants dans les extraits :
- Le projet vise à **renforcer la planification et la mise en œuvre des politiques/programmes/projets des secteurs eau et agriculture** en intégrant les risques climatiques [105_gcf-b30-02-add02, p. 21].  
- Il prévoit de développer un **Climate Information Service (CIS)** pour la **gestion de l’eau** et la **planification des moyens de subsistance agricoles**, avec diffusion d’informations/projections adaptées aux besoins locaux pour informer les pratiques d’irrigation et la planification agricole au niveau des exploitations [105_gcf-b30-02-add02, p. 21].  
- Des activités de **renforcement de capacités et de formation technique** (par ex. formation de personnels d’agences thaïlandaises sur l’intégration du changement climatique dans la gestion des ressources en eau) appuient cette approche [105_gcf-b30-02-add02, p. 97].  
- Le document cite explicitement le **riz** dans ses références (“Thai rice”) [105_gcf-b30-02-add02, p. 12], mais les extraits récupérés ne détaillent pas une composante “riziculture” dédiée.

# INTRODUCTION

Une mission d'évaluation du Programme Régional de Financement de l'Adaptation au Niveau local (LoCAL) en Afrique du Ouest (Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Mali et Niger) a débuté le 16 au 27 mai 2024 à Ouagadougou au Burkina Faso. Cette mission est réalisée par l'IFAD, impliquant que toutes modifications du Document Complet de Projet (DCP) doivent être portées à la connaissance des parties prenantes avant effet. La mission d'évaluation circulaire, qui a donc été conduite dans cette logique avec une attention particulière pour le cadre institutionnel et la gouvernance, est menée par Mme Aïda Héménière, Projets Climat (SDPC), accompagnée pour l'étude du Burkina Faso par M. Abdoul Aziz Ouédraogo, Responsable du Commissariat des développements de projets au sein du Bureau Régional du Projet LoCAL.

## PROGRAMME RÉGIONAL DE FINANCEMENT DE L'ADAPTATION AU NIVEAU LOCAL

Le Programme Régional de Financement de l'Adaptation au Niveau Local (LoCAL) HRM est décliné autour de deux composantes, à savoir : [i] le renforcement des capacités de sensibilisation et de communication locales pour favoriser la prise en compte des risques climatiques dans les stratégies d'adaptation locales et ii) l'établissement de mécanismes de financement basés sur le pays pour soutenir l'investissement local. Les domaines d'intervention du programme sont : [i] la gestion des ressources naturelles localement menacées par la réchauffement climatique, les inondations et les sécheresses ; [ii] la transition énergétique vers une économie basée sur l'énergie renouvelable, les infrastructures résilientes au climat et les zones côtières.

Les mesures clés du programme visent à : [i] renforcer les capacités institutionnelles, techniques et financières au niveau local ; (ii) réduire le coût des coûts supplémentaires des investissements résilients au climat ; (iii) la mise en œuvre d'initiatives pilotes pour l'évaluation de l'impact des interventions sur les écosystèmes, le secteur privé local et gérer des investissements alignés sur les priorités d'adaptation.

## 2.2 Equitable access to finance for bio-businesses in the Amazon

Equitable access to finance is a key element of the GCF’s strategy to increase global investment flows to early-stage bio-businesses in the Amazon region in the form of direct equity, equity-like instruments and other financial products. The GCF will provide funding through its own funds under administration by the IDB (such as IDB Lab) and other co-finance. These schemes are considered effective tools to maximize the potential impact of financing operations in early-stage high-potential bio-businesses. They can be used for both equity investments and equity-like investments while offering more value for innovative companies. Equity will be used for more mature bio-businesses (i.e., those that have already demonstrated a proof-of-concept or are at an earlier viable product phase), have positive revenues, and are looking for gaining market traction.

## Programme implementation risk

Within the four target countries, there is limited institutional capacity and skill set in the dairy industry including dairy technicians, social / gender equality awareness, project management skills, and financial management. This may lead to project delays. This is being mitigated by competitive recruitment of qualified project management staff and a robust monitoring system.

## Programme's concessional pricing

To ensure that full benefit of concessional loan pricing under Component 3 is passed on to end borrowers, the facility agreements will include provisions for interest rate floors. The interest rate floor will be set at 5% per annum. This will be reduced by the lowered funding cost from this programme compared to the retail banks' own funding costs.

Despite the fact that Argentina ranks in the middle of the Index of Environmental Risk Exposure (World Bank, 2005), exposure to such risk increases because of the large number of people living in vulnerable areas (prevailing poverty and lack of access to basic services). The country has shown specific climatic characteristics in large part of its territory, most likely associated with climate changes. Those characteristics were the cause of certain type of disasters in sectors such as energy and agriculture. Broadly speaking, these are: (i) an increase in average temperature; (ii) a decrease in precipitation; (iii) more frequent heavy rains; (iv) higher frequency of heat waves; (v) increased evaporation rates; (vi) lower humidity; (vii) reduced temperatures of 1°C or less during the Southern part.

- **Component 2:** Conduct a cost-benefit analysis to assess the potential and viability of such interventions for increasing the grid resilience

### Component 1: Increase climate resilience of urban transport infrastructure

The outcome of this component is (1) Urban transport system less vulnerable to climate extremes.

To increase climate resilience of the EUITS, it is important to understand the climatic hazards conditions at which its infrastructure is exposed and how vulnerable it is to climate stresses. The design and implementation of climate resilient transport infrastructure can provide such measures that mitigate the risk of transport systems failure. Then, the Program will develop a cost-benefit analysis methodology for assessing the potential and viability of such interventions.
such measures that mitigate the risk of transport systems failure. Then, the Program will develop a cost-benefit analysis methodology for assessing the potential and viability of such interventions.

The proposed methodology is based on the following steps: (1) A qualitative disaster and climate change risk assessment for the EUITS (see Annex 2). This step includes an evaluation of the vulnerability of the transport system to extreme weather events. (2) An economic analysis for the pre-feasibility stage of the implementation of urban interventions considered as adaptation measures, including a cost-benefit analysis methodology. The proposed methodology will be applied in two scenarios: under climate change scenarios and adaptation alternatives, for (i) the network of routes of the bus system and (ii) the network of routes of the metro system.
ology will be applied in two scenarios: under climate change scenarios and adaptation alternatives, for (i) the network of routes of the bus system and (ii) the network of routes of the metro system. The economic analysis will include an evaluation of the costs associated with considering nature-based solutions, which can be derived from projects underway in the city. The methodology defines climate resilient transport infrastructure as a set of measures that are designed to reduce the vulnerability of the EUITS to extreme weather events and other hazards. These measures should be integrated along the route and its components (terminals and stations) and make an economic evaluation of the costs associated with considering nature-based solutions, which can be derived from projects underway in the city's public transport system.

### 130 Settlements in Tonga, are concentrated in coastal areas with significant percentages of the population living and earning their livelihood along the coast. The majority of the settlements are located on low-lying islands, which are vulnerable to sea-level rise, storm surges, and tsunamis. These natural hazards have been exacerbated by climate change, including increased frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones, sea level rise, and coastal erosion caused by flooding during storms. Moreover, freshwater resources are negatively impacted by sea-level rise and increased salinity in the aquifers. The vulnerability is further compounded by Tonga’s low-lying islands, characterized by their small land area with low elevation.

### Impacts and benefits of the RSF

- The RSF includes targeted credit enhancement and risk sharing. It specifically targets loans to MSME CSG borrowers, reducing risk for PFIs by guaranteeing 50% of each firm’s exposure on a pari-passu basis. This mechanism directly addresses the high-risk nature of MSME lending, which typically has shorter terms (e.g., three to six months). In case of defaults, losses are shared between the RSF and the PFI, ensuring that the financial burden does not fall solely on the lender.

- The RSF design builds on precedents from existing MSME-focused guarantee schemes in India and enhances these with a clear focus on CSG projects. Existing schemes such as the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGFT) have been successful, but they are often underfunded and lack sufficient capacity to absorb large-scale participation. Beyond direct financial support, the RSF serves as a market-making tool. As banks gain confidence from successful transactions in lending, the overall risk perception of the MSME CSG sector is expected to decline, paving the way for additional financial incentives in the future.

The project consists of 3 inter-related components:

- Component 2: Improving Grid Absorption Capacity followed by PV deployment
- Component 3: PV mini-grids on the Outer Island of Agalega

# Annexe 03 : Arrangement Institutionnel du Programme LoCAL au Burkina Faso

## Catégorisation du projet au niveau national

Sur le plan national, en fonction de leur rattachement et de leur mode de gestion, les projets et programmes de développement sont classés en quatre (4) catégories. Les catégories applicables au présent projet sont les suivantes :

- **Catégorie 1 : Projet exécuté directement par l'administration publique** ;
- **Catégorie 2 : Projet nécessitant pour sa mise en œuvre, la création d'une structure autonome d'exécution placée sous la tutelle de l'administration publique.**

En regard des critères de classification et dans un souci d'efficacité, le choix s'est porté sur la catégorie 2 : Projet nécessitant pour sa mise en œuvre la création d'une structure autonome d'exécution placée sous la tutelle de l'administration publique.

## Entité d'exécution et Unité de Gestion du Projet (UGP)
jet nécessitant pour sa mise en œuvre la création d'une structure autonome d'exécution placée sous la tutelle de l'administration publique.

## Entité d'exécution et Unité de Gestion du Projet (UGP)

Au Burkina Faso, l'entité d'exécution (EE) du projet est le Fonds d'Intervention pour l'Environnement (FIE), un Fonds d'Etat sous la tutelle technique du Ministère de l'Environnement, de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement (MEEA). La principale mission du FIE est de contribuer à la réalisation des objectifs environnementaux du Burkina Faso, notamment la réduction de la dégradation de l'environnement et des pertes économiques associées, ainsi que la lutte contre les effets négatifs du changement climatique. Par ailleurs, le FIE est un instrument financier robuste capable de mobiliser des financements nationaux et internationaux pour soutenir l'atteinte des objectifs environnementaux.

- Leveraging information and communication technologies for more sustainable agriculture.
- Digging smart irrigation systems to sustain crop yields.
- Facilitating access to financing for small farmers and cooperatives to reduce food losses.
- Improving storage techniques and providing training on post-harvest management.

## Secrétariat technique LOCAL

Dans le cadre du déploiement du Météorème LoCAL au Burkina Faso, il a été mis en place un Comité technique LoCAL par arrêté n°T368/MEAT/CAL du 14 juillet 2022 portant création, attributions et composition d'un Comité Technique du LoCAL de financement de l'adaptation au changement climatique et météorème local à LoCAL (Météorème LoCAL au Burkina Faso). La mission principale de ce Comité est de coordonner et de suivre la mise en œuvre du Météorème LoCAL au Burkina Faso. Placé sous la présidence du FIE, ce comité dispose d'un Secrétariat technique composé de membres désignés du FIE, de l'Autorité Nationale Désignée du Fonds vert pour le climat (ANDFPC), de la Direction Générale du Développement Territorial (DGDT) et de la Direction Générale des Collectivités Territoriales (DGT).
e l'Autorité Nationale Désignée du Fonds vert pour le climat (ANDFPC), de la Direction Générale du Développement Territorial (DGDT) et de la Direction Générale des Collectivités Territoriales (DGT).

A ces structures, il conviendra d'ajouter la Direction Générale de la Coopération (DGCOOP) et l'Agence Nationale d'Aide au Développement des Collectivités Territoriales (ADACT). Dans le cadre du présent projet, le Comité technique LoCAL en collaboration avec l'UOP pour l'alignement des différents documents/livraisons avec le marché de la construction, a décidé de créer un CPT. Il collaborera avec l'UOP pour lever les goulots d'étranglement qui pourrait entraver la mise en œuvre du projet. Pour finir, le secrétariat technique contribuera à la consolidation des documents préparés par l'UOP avant transmission au Comité de Pilotage (COPIL) qui est composé de la majorité des membres du Comité Technique LoCAL.

### Comité de pilotage (COPIL)
consolidation des documents préparés par l'UOP avant transmission au Comité de Pilotage (COPIL) qui est composé de la majorité des membres du Comité Technique LoCAL.

### Comité de pilotage (COPIL)

Afin de faciliter la mise en œuvre du projet, un Comité de Pilotage (COPIL) sera mis en place conformément aux dispositions du décret n°2013-1389/RES/PAM/MEF du 31 décembre 2013 portant réglementation générale des projets et programmes de développement exécutés au Burkina Faso. Le COPIL sert d'organe d'orientation et de pilotage du projet. Le COPIL se réunira en session ordinaire deux (02) fois par an pour superviser la mise en œuvre du projet et renrer compte des progrès accomplis, il peut toutefois se réunir en session extraordinaire sur convocation du son Président.

Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, le COPIL est composé de membres statutaires et de membres observateurs.
